Karl pressed a glittering piece of ore into a handful of mud, hoping the shine might rub off and improve the mud's prospects. The mud stayed exactly as plain and sticky as before, decoration or not. The ore has a future waiting for it; the mud has, at best, an afternoon.
I know exactly what this ore was actually glittering for today, and it was not to decorate a handful of mud. The ore is the future, patiently; the mud just got a bit of grit stuck in it.
Karl scattered a handful of dry grass across the boules pitch for cushioning, in case a throw ever went badly. It only blew about in the wind, and Ugh eventually stepped in it and complained.

The rules of boules ask for a flat court and one very particular stone. Dry grass offers neither, being light, dry, and prone to blowing away mid-game. The court stayed exactly as bare as those rules require.
Two mud pies now, and Karl has already finished the first and started on the second before the narrator can even file a complaint about the first.
Karl held one mud pie up next to another, as if quality might improve through comparison shopping. Both were equally edible, equally muddy, and gone within the same disappointing minute.

Karl jabbed the spear into a patch of mud, testing the edge the way he tests everything sharp. Sharp needs resistance to mean anything, and the mud, soft and sticky and entirely without opinions, gave none at all.
Sharp and pointed met soft and sticky, and sharp lost immediately: the spear went in, came out coated, and proved nothing except that mud swallows an edge whole.

The cave painting is berry juice, dried onto stone years ago, and finished being whatever it is. Karl stacked a mud brick up beside it anyway, hoping architecture and art might strike up a conversation. They did not.

Two mud bricks make Karl an architect, by his own generous assessment. Zero mud bricks make a cave painting, which was built from crushed berries and patience instead. The two crafts never once needed each other's materials.

The standing stone has meant something, probably, for longer than Karl has been alive to wonder about it. Berry juice means dinner, or a stain, or occasionally both. Karl poured one over the base of the other, and history recorded no further ceremony.

I checked for a connection between the standing stone and a cup of berry juice. I found a monument that predates memory, and a drink that stains everything within an arm's reach. Nothing carried over from one to the other.

Karl weighed the hand axe in his palm, wondering if a blade might improve on berry juice as a medium. It could not — the cave painting was already finished, sacred, and entirely uninterested in further editing.
The cave painting finished being made the moment Karl stepped back and refused to explain it. The hand axe, quietly competent as ever, had nothing left to cut there, and nothing left to prove either.
Now there are two of the same cave gallery standing in camp, each with its own careful pair of paintings, and Karl paces between them, unsure which deserves the finger-width adjustment first.

Karl set one cave gallery beside the other cave gallery, hoping for a verdict on which curation was superior. Both were, by his own exacting standard, perfect. Neither was more perfect than the other.

Karl scattered a handful of seeds across a shower of sparks, hoping heat might finally explain what they were for. The sparks died before the seeds even warmed through, and the mystery stayed exactly as unsolved as before. The seeds was going to answer that question eventually; this was not the afternoon.

I know exactly what these seeds are actually waiting for, and it is not a shower of sparks that vanish before the question even finishes. The seeds gives them the actual time they need; the sparks lasted one bright moment and left the seeds exactly as they were.

Karl offered the cave gallery a fresh cup of berry juice, in case the two paintings wanted retouching. They were dry, sacred, and finished years before this particular cup existed, and it only dripped down the wall instead.

Berry juice, once dried, becomes exactly this: pigment fixed to stone, permanent, no longer liquid. What Karl carried into the cave gallery was still very much a drink. Permanent things and a drink don't have much use for each other.

By rights, a net and enough rope should very nearly build each other — one is, after all, just the other with holes tied in correctly. Karl twisted the rope around itself for a good while and produced only a very committed knot.

I apologise to the rope, and I apologise to the net, which is, by its own description, just rope with the holes done properly. Today the doing-properly part stayed stubbornly out of reach, and neither material was to blame.

Karl held his glittering ore up beside 'the good rock,' half expecting one treasure to recognise the other. The round stone stayed exactly as guarded and ordinary as ever, unmoved by a rival with a better future ahead of it. The ore was worth guarding; the other never entered this contest.

I know exactly which of these Karl will still be digging up in a few centuries, and it isn't the round stone he already polished smooth and started guarding jealously. The ore of the ore and the round stone is patient about being valuable; the other one already peaked.
Two mud baths now, side by side, and Karl can only be in one of them at a time. The boar approves of both equally, which is not the same as either one being more useful.
Karl rolled from one mud bath into the identical one beside it, hoping for a change of scenery. Both were the same mud, the same wet, the same boar nodding the same approval.
The cave painting stays exactly where Karl left it, sacred and unmoving, forever. The wheel has already escaped down the valley twice today and shows no intention of holding still for a portrait.
Karl chased the wheel back from the valley a third time and set it down in front of the cave painting, hoping stillness might be contagious. The wheel rolled off again before the lesson could take.
Karl pressed the round stone into the spear, hoping proximity might count for something. It did not. The round stone belongs with the {partner}; this meeting was merely in the way.
The round stone rolled, the spear pointed, and neither talent helped the other. Somewhere else, the {partner} can actually use the round stone. History recommends they meet there.
Karl rolled the water toward the boules court, expecting a splash to count as a legal throw. Nobody agreed, least of all the boules, which do not get wet on principle.
There is no rule in boules that rewards proximity to the water, and Karl checked twice before accepting that his afternoon's strategy did not exist.
Karl dipped the ore in the berry juice, waiting for a shine that never arrived. Rock does not drink, and rock especially does not drink fruit.
The ore sat in a puddle of berry juice for the length of an entire afternoon, gaining nothing but a faint purple tinge Karl mistook for progress.
Karl struck the stone axe with the hammer, hoping one finished tool might improve the other. It did not. The hammer belongs with the {partner}; this was only tools comparing handles.
The hammer and the stone axe met as two professionals forced into the same meeting. Somewhere else, the {partner} has legitimate work for the hammer. The other brought opinions.
Karl leaned the mud brick against the standing stone like an offering, unsure which of them was meant to be impressed.
The standing stone has stood, unmoved and unimpressed, since before Karl learned to stack mud bricks. It remained exactly that unimpressed today.
Karl held a lump of ore up to the cave painting, checking if the glitter matched anything already drawn. It matched nothing; the painting had never once depicted rocks.
The cave painting depicts a boar, a sunset, or possibly Ugh, depending entirely on who is asked. Ore was never a candidate, and today's introduction did not change that.
Karl pointed the spear at the cave painting as though scoring a very slow hit. The painting did not flinch, being made of stone and mineral pigment, not boar.
There is a version of the cave painting where the spear appears, and Karl has not painted it yet. Holding the actual spear up to the actual painting changed nothing about that.
Karl struck the hand axe against nothing in particular, hoping the sparks might improve its edge. The edge stayed exactly as sharp, and exactly as unimproved by fire it never touched.
Sparks live for half a second and then are gone; the hand axe has outlasted several of Karl's other tools by years. Introducing the two taught neither of them anything about the other.
The spear is built for exactly this: something fast, wet, and worth catching. Karl held it over the fish for a long moment, certain a recipe was one thrust away.
Every instinct Karl has says the spear and the fish belong together, one hunting the other in some obvious way he can't yet name. The moment came and went without becoming anything.
Karl looped the rope around the spear and waited for cleverness. The knot held; history did not. The rope belongs with the {partner}, not today's volunteer.
The rope and the spear produced a very secure version of nothing. Somewhere else, the {partner} can make proper use of the rope. This pairing merely tied up the afternoon.
Karl offered the stick to the boules court as a replacement rule, on the grounds that sticks are sometimes involved in games. They are not involved in this one.
There is a stick at the center of every boules match, the one Ugh throws for, and it is never the stick Karl happened to be holding. Today's stick was no exception.
Karl held up two hammers side by side, checking whether one had grown sharper out of sheer jealousy. Neither had. They remain, stubbornly, the same hammer twice.
Two hammers, introduced to each other with great ceremony, discovered they had absolutely nothing new to say. Karl's arm, already upgraded once by the hammer, did not get a second upgrade.
Karl held the fire near the stone axe, expecting heat to improve an edge already proud of itself. It did not. The fire belongs with the {partner}; the other only got warm.
Fire met the stone axe and discovered that finished tools are poor raw material. Somewhere else, the {partner} can still do useful work with the fire. Here, nothing changed.
The boomerang and the spear are cut from the same reliable wood, and Karl felt sure that shared material meant a shared future. It didn't, not yet.
Karl weighed the boomerang against the spear, both wood, both familiar in his hand, and waited for the obvious idea to finish forming. It never quite did.
Karl set up two boules courts side by side, hoping a rematch might change eleven straight losses. It changed nothing; the boules stayed exactly as merciless as before.
There is only one set of boules Karl actually owns, and introducing it to itself did not produce a second, easier opponent. Ugh remains undefeated either way.
Karl set the round stone beside the cave gallery, hoping placement alone might make it art. It did not. The cave gallery belongs with the {partner}; the other can wait outside the exhibition.
The cave gallery considered the round stone for a full second and declined the submission. Somewhere else, the {partner} has actual business with the cave gallery. This arrangement did not.
Karl held the fire close to the cave painting to see it better, then remembered what fire does to things that took him all afternoon to draw and stepped back immediately.
The cave painting has survived every previous evening by staying far from the fire, and tonight was not the night that policy changed.

The digging stick is built for exactly one job — turning ground into something workable — and the clay underneath it is about as workable as ground ever gets. Karl felt the idea arrive and then, somehow, leave again.
Karl pressed the digging stick into the clay, certain that a tool this good and a material this soft owed each other something more than a hole. Nothing more arrived today.
Karl baited the snare with berry juice, on the theory that anything sticky counts as bait. The snare caught nothing but a faint purple stain and Karl's own optimism.
A snare hunts quietly while Karl sleeps; berry juice does nothing while anyone sleeps. Combining the two taught the snare nothing about patience it didn't already have.
The hand axe can shape almost anything Karl hands it, and seeds turned out to be the smallest, least cooperative thing he's tried so far. Something should come of that eventually.
Karl set the hand axe next to a small pile of seeds, waiting for shape to happen to something that doesn't hold still. Seeds, it turns out, do not hold still for good reasons.
Karl rolled the wheel past the spear, admiring one motion and the other's point. Together, they invented traffic. The wheel belongs with the {partner}; this crossing was merely inconvenient.

The wheel and the spear each arrived with a perfectly respectable purpose, neither involving the other. Somewhere else, the {partner} has a working future with the wheel. Today's meeting was a scheduling error.
Karl held the fire close to the round stone, hoping heat might persuade polish into progress. It did not. The fire belongs with the {partner}; the other remained decorative.
The round stone warmed up. The fire used fire. Civilisation remained exactly where it was. Somewhere else, the {partner} has better work for the fire, away from this lukewarm summit.
Karl poured the berry juice near the fire, expecting steam or spectacle. It hissed once and stopped. The fire belongs with the {partner}; the other was only dampening the mood.
Fire and berry juice held a brief meeting about heat, sweetness, and neither one's actual job. Somewhere else, the {partner} has useful plans for the fire. This was refreshments.
Karl rolled the wheel through the mud, expecting the track to become an invention. It became a track. The wheel belongs with the {partner}; this route went nowhere.
The mud clung to the wheel with real commitment and no useful result. Somewhere else, the {partner} has a working future with the wheel. The other merely needs cleaning.
The mud brick and the round stone are both hard, both stubborn, both convinced they belong in a wall somewhere. Karl held them together and waited for the wall to agree.
Karl stacked the round stone on top of the mud brick, testing whether hard-and-heavy and hard-and-dry might finally add up to something standing. Not today, but the idea has legs.
Sparks fly. Karl gasps. I gasp. The boar leaps away fast.

Karl smiled once. The boar wandered off slowly.
Karl waits. The fire catches. Nothing else moves here tonight.
Bronze!
Karl pauses—waits—then: nothing. Nothing at all... just silence, and more silence.
What was that? Did it move? Karl is not sure anymore.
